title: Fashion and Clothes
description: Ten stories and short texts about clothes and the people who make, mend, choose and remember them: a grandmother's sewing machine, a tailor, a used-clothing store, a young designer, a school uniform debate, a wedding dress and more.

lessons.title: My Grandmother's Sewing Machine
lessons.summary: Anna receives her grandmother's old mechanical sewing machine and slowly learns to use it.
lessons.text:
When my grandmother Ruth moved into a smaller apartment last spring, she gave me her sewing machine. It is a heavy black machine with gold letters on its side, and it is older than my mother. Ruth bought it in 1968 with the money from her first job, and for more than 50 years it was her constant companion. It made every school dress and every birthday shirt in the family.

The machine is completely mechanical. There are no screens and no lights. When you press down with your foot, the wheel turns and the whole table shakes with a slight, regular rhythm. To me, that mechanical sound is the sound of my childhood.

At first I did not know how to use it, but the original manual was still in the drawer, its pages soft and yellow with age. Ruth had written notes in the manual in blue ink. Next to the page about the tension of the thread, she had written: "Be patient. Test on a small piece first."

Tension, I soon learned, is everything. If the tension is too tight, the material pulls. If it is too loose, the thread makes ugly loops under the material. I spent a whole Saturday making slight changes to a small wheel and testing each one on an old towel.

Every evening I called Ruth, and she gave me a hint or two. "Listen to the machine," was her favorite hint. "When it sounds happy, the tension is right." It seemed like strange advice, but after a week I could hear the difference.

Ruth's old machine is also more reliable than any modern one. In 50 years it has never needed a repair, except for a drop of oil now and then. A reliable machine, she says, is one that you can forget about, because it simply works.

For me, the machine is more than a tool. It is part of our family heritage, like the old photographs on my mother's wall. One day I want to pass this heritage on to my daughter, together with the manual and its blue notes.

Last Sunday I finished my first real project: a simple summer dress for Ruth. When she put it on, she stood in front of the mirror for a long time. "You see, Anna," she said, "the machine remembers." I am deeply grateful to her, not only for the machine but also for her patience. And I think she is grateful, too, that her old companion has found a new home.

Questions:
Why did Ruth give her sewing machine to Anna?
She gave it to her because she moved into a smaller apartment.
What happens when you press down with your foot?
The wheel turns and the whole table shakes with a slight, regular rhythm.
What had Ruth written in the manual next to the page about tension?
She had written: "Be patient. Test on a small piece first."
What was Ruth's favorite hint?
Her favorite hint was "Listen to the machine."
Why is the machine so reliable?
In 50 years it has never needed a repair, except for a drop of oil.
What was Anna's first real project?
It was a simple summer dress for Ruth.

lessons.title: The Tailor on Northeast Avenue
lessons.summary: A quiet professor visits an old tailor to order a suit for a ceremony at his university.
lessons.text:
In the northeast corner of the old town there is a narrow shop with a green door. A small sign above the window says: "Mr. Novak, Tailor." The shop has been there for roughly 40 years, and Mr. Novak has worked in it for all of them.

One gray morning in October, a tall man with white hair came in. His name was Daniel Hayes, and he was a history professor at the university in the northeast part of the city. In two weeks, the faculty was going to hold a ceremony for its graduating students, and every member of the faculty had to look his or her best.

"I am afraid clothes are not my strength," the professor said. "I have spent my life with books. I own roughly three jackets, and all of them are brown."

Mr. Novak smiled. He liked customers with a sense of humor, and he could see plenty of humor behind the professor's serious glasses.

The tailor took out his measuring tape and measured the professor's shoulders, arms and back. Then he showed him several materials. "This one is genuine wool," he said. "Feel it. Genuine wool lets the air through, so you will not be too warm under the lights."

While the professor looked at the samples, Mr. Novak picked up his scissors. They were large and heavy, with long silver blades. Before he cut anything, he always wiped the blades with a soft towel, slowly, the way another man might wipe his glasses. "Sharp blades and clean blades," he said. "That is the first rule of a tailor."

The professor watched with interest. He was an intellectual, a man who loved ideas and questions. "Is there an intellectual side to your work?" he asked.

"Of course," said Mr. Novak. "Every suit is a small puzzle. And every customer is a different puzzle."

At the end of the visit, the professor chose a dark blue material. He also bought a brown leather belt, because the tailor sold a few leather goods as well. Mr. Novak wrote the order by hand, and the professor added his signature at the bottom. His signature was long and beautiful, almost like a drawing.

Two weeks later, the professor wore the new suit at the ceremony. Afterward, he came back to the shop with a box of chocolates. Mr. Novak wiped his hands, opened the box and smiled. "Now," he said with his usual humor, "you own four jackets, and one of them is blue."

Questions:
Where is Mr. Novak's shop?
It is in the northeast corner of the old town.
Why did Professor Hayes need a suit?
He needed it because the faculty was going to hold a ceremony for its graduating students.
What does Mr. Novak always do before he cuts anything?
He always wipes the blades of his scissors with a soft towel.
Why did the tailor recommend genuine wool?
He recommended it because genuine wool lets the air through.
What did the professor add at the bottom of the order?
He added his signature, which was long and beautiful.
How many jackets does the professor own now?
He owns four jackets, and one of them is blue.

lessons.title: The Powder Blue Coat
lessons.summary: Maya finds a powder blue coat at a used-clothing store and gives it new buttons.
lessons.text:
Every Saturday morning, Maya Brooks goes to the same place: a large used-clothing store on Pine Street called Second Chance. The store sells clothes that people have given away. Maya is 24, and she has not bought a new piece of clothing in two years.

The store is not beautiful. The lights are bright, the floor is old, and the air smells slightly of soap and dust. To Maya, however, it is full of possibilities. She loves the diversity of the place. A farmer's heavy coat hangs next to an evening dress. No ordinary store has such diversity, because every piece has a past and no two pieces are the same.

Maya does not look at the clothes slowly, one by one. She rifles through them quickly, the way a person rifles through a drawer in search of lost keys. When something catches her eye, she stops and pulls it out.

At the back of the store stands a big old barrel full of buttons from clothes that were too damaged to sell. For a dollar, you can fill a small bag from the barrel. Maya likes to push her hands deep into it and feel the buttons run between her fingers: glass, metal, wood and horn. Horn buttons are her favorite. They are made from the horns of cows, and each one has its own pattern of light and dark lines.

This Saturday, Maya found a wool coat in a soft powder blue, the color of a spring morning. Inside, it had a brighter blue lining. Its color reminded her of a robin that had once built its nest in her parents' garden. The robin had laid 3 small eggs of exactly that blue. The coat had a small stain on the front, and three of its buttons were missing, but it cost only 12 dollars.

At the counter, Maya talked to Mr. Lopez, the old man who runs the store. He sorts every donation himself. "This coat came in a donation last week," he said. "Before winter, the number of donations triples, so I have to triple the number of volunteers."

"Do you know anything about stain removal?" Maya asked.

"Cold water and patience," Mr. Lopez answered. "Hot water makes stain removal much harder, because it fixes the stain in the material."

At home, Maya followed his advice, and the stain came out. Then she found the right buttons in her bag: three horn buttons in the soft gray of ash. Against the powder blue coat, the ash gray buttons looked as if they had always been there.

Questions:
What does Second Chance sell?
It sells clothes that people have given away.
Why does Maya love the diversity of the store?
Because every piece has a past and no two pieces are the same.
What is in the barrel at the back of the store?
It is full of buttons from clothes that were too damaged to sell.
What did the color of the lining remind Maya of?
It reminded her of the eggs of a robin in her parents' garden.
What did Mr. Lopez say about stain removal?
He said that you need cold water and patience.
Which buttons did Maya choose for the coat?
She chose three horn buttons in the soft gray of ash.

lessons.title: The Final Assignment
lessons.summary: A design student works hard on a jacket for his final assignment and learns that a simple idea is often best.
lessons.text:
Leo Park was in his first year at a design school. In March, his teacher, Ms. Grant, gave the class their final assignment. Each student had to make one jacket from old clothes, and three teachers would evaluate the results at the end of the month.

"When we evaluate your work," Ms. Grant explained, "we will look at two things: the idea and the execution. A brilliant idea with poor execution is still a poor jacket."

Leo was excited. That evening he filled 20 pages with drawings. His idea was a long jacket made from 6 different old shirts, with pockets of every shape and color. He felt like a genius.

The execution, however, was much harder than the drawing. The shirts were made of different materials, so they did not fit together well. Every evening Leo cut, pinned and measured until late at night. After two weeks, he was exhausted. One night his roommate found him asleep at the kitchen table, with his head on a pile of shirts. It was the third time that week that Leo had fallen asleep there.

Four days before the end of the month, Leo looked at the jacket and began to panic. It did not look like a design at all. The colors fought with each other, and the pockets went in every direction. In a panic, he called his older sister, who was a designer.

His sister listened to everything. "Stop for a moment," she said. "Who is the creator of this jacket, you or your drawings? A good creator listens to the material. What does the jacket want to be?"

That was the insight that Leo needed. He realized that he had tried to do too much. He removed 4 of the 6 shirts and kept only two: one in dark blue and one in light gray. He coordinated the two colors carefully and gave all the pockets the same simple shape. Suddenly, the jacket looked calm and clear.

On the day the teachers evaluated the jackets, Leo was still a little exhausted, but he was no longer in a panic. Ms. Grant studied his jacket for a long time. "The colors are well coordinated," she said, "and the execution is clean. What changed?"

Leo told her about his sister's insight. Ms. Grant smiled. "Nobody here is a genius, Leo," she said. "But a creator who can take things away is worth more than a genius who only adds."

That night, Leo went to bed at nine and was asleep in five minutes.

Questions:
What was the final assignment?
Each student had to make one jacket from old clothes.
What would the teachers look at when they evaluated the jackets?
They would look at the idea and the execution.
Where did Leo's roommate find him asleep?
He found him asleep at the kitchen table.
Why did Leo panic four days before the end of the month?
He panicked because the colors fought with each other.
What insight did Leo's sister give him?
She told him that a good creator listens to the material.
How did Leo change the jacket?
He kept only two shirts with coordinated colors and gave the pockets the same simple shape.

lessons.title: Should Our School Adopt a Uniform?
lessons.summary: A parent weighs the arguments for and against school uniforms in a calm newspaper column.
lessons.text:
Should Our School Adopt a Uniform?
By Helen Ward

Last month, the school board of Maple Grove High School declared that it would make a decision about school uniforms by the end of the year. Should our school adopt a uniform, or should students be free to wear what they like? As a mother of two, I have thought about it a lot.

First, I must admit my own bias. I wore a uniform at school for 12 years, and I remember it as gray and boring. Because of this bias, I began with a strong feeling against uniforms. However, a feeling is not an argument, so I tried to look at the question with some logic.

The strongest argument for a uniform is equity. When every student wears the same clothes, nobody is judged by the price of his or her shoes. Families do not have to buy expensive brands merely so that their children feel accepted. For families with little money, this kind of equity matters greatly.

The second argument comes from psychology. Some studies in psychology suggest that clothes influence the way we act. A uniform, according to this idea, tells students that school is a place for work. I find this logic interesting, although I am not sure that a tie can make anyone study harder.

Now imagine a different scenario. A girl loves color, and her clothes are one of the few ways she can show who she is. If the school adopts a uniform, she loses that small freedom. In this scenario, a uniform is not merely a piece of clothing; it is a message that every student should look the same.

A uniform is cheap only if the school chooses simple clothes that families can buy in ordinary stores. If the school declares that every jacket must come from one special company, the cost could greatly increase, and the argument of equity would lose its force.

Before the board decides, I hope it will carry out a comprehensive survey. A comprehensive survey should ask parents, teachers and, above all, students, since they are the people who will wear the uniform every day.

My own view has changed. I no longer think that uniforms are simply a bad idea. Provided that the uniform is cheap, comfortable and chosen together with the students, I would support it. Unless those conditions are met, I would rather keep our freedom of dress.

Questions:
What did the school board declare last month?
It declared that it would make a decision about uniforms by the end of the year.
What bias does Helen Ward admit?
She admits that she began with a strong feeling against uniforms.
Why is equity the strongest argument for a uniform?
Because nobody is judged by the price of his or her shoes.
What does the scenario of the girl who loves color show?
It shows that a uniform can take away a small freedom to show who you are.
Who should a comprehensive survey ask?
It should ask parents, teachers and, above all, students.
Under what conditions would Helen support a uniform?
She would support it if it were cheap, comfortable and chosen together with the students.

lessons.title: The Simple Dress
lessons.summary: Emma and her sister look for a wedding dress and find a simple one that feels right.
lessons.text:
Emma and Sam announced their engagement at Christmas, and the wedding was planned for the following September. Their engagement was not a surprise to anyone, since they had been together for six years. Their romance had begun in a library, over a book that they both wanted to borrow. Choosing a dress, however, turned out to be surprisingly difficult.

On a gray Saturday in April, she went shopping with her older sister, Kate. Kate was in the sixth month of her pregnancy and got tired quickly, so they planned to visit only two shops. Dark clouds threatened rain all morning.

The first shop was large, bright and full of people. Mirrors covered every wall, and three other young women were trying on dresses at the same time. The woman who helped Emma spoke very fast. She talked about romance and about "the most important day of your life." After half an hour, Emma felt a strong desire to flee. "I can't think in here," she told Kate.

They fled into a small coffee shop across the street just as the first drops began to fall. Kate put her feet up on a chair, because her doctor had told her to rest often during the pregnancy.

"Tell me what you really want," Kate said.

Emma thought for a long time. "I don't need an extraordinary dress," she said at last. "Those dresses were extraordinary, but I felt as if I were wearing a costume. I want something simple. Something that feels like me."

An hour later, the rain was lighter, although the sky still threatened more. The second shop was small and calm. It belonged to Mrs. Silva, an older woman who made many of the dresses herself. She gave Emma a private fitting room, and Emma was grateful for the privacy. In the first shop there had been no privacy at all.

The third dress she tried on was soft, white and completely plain. When Emma stepped out of the fitting room, Kate did not say anything. She just put her hand to her mouth. Emma looked in the mirror and felt something tight in her throat. She tried to speak, but her throat was too tight for words.

Mrs. Silva smiled. "That is the one," she said. "I always know."

Kate stood up slowly and gave her sister a long hug. It was not easy, because of the baby between them, and both women started to laugh. It was the warmest hug of the day. Outside, the sun had come out, and for the first time since Christmas, the wedding felt real.

Questions:
When did Emma and Sam announce their engagement?
They announced their engagement at Christmas.
Why did the sisters plan to visit only two shops?
Because Kate was pregnant and got tired quickly.
Why did Emma want to flee from the first shop?
She wanted to flee because the shop was crowded and the woman spoke very fast.
What did Emma say she wanted?
She said she did not need an extraordinary dress; she wanted something simple.
Why was Emma grateful in the second shop?
She was grateful for the privacy of the fitting room.
What did Kate do when she saw Emma in the plain dress?
She gave her sister a long hug.

lessons.title: A Servant's Dress
lessons.summary: A museum worker describes a plain work dress that the museum bought at an auction.
lessons.text:
I have worked in the clothing collection of the Riverton City Museum for 15 years. Our museum is affiliated with the state university, and being affiliated with a university means that we do not only show old clothes; we also study them. Let me tell you about our newest acquisition.

In June, we bought a dress at an auction in Boston. Most dresses sold at such auctions once belonged to rich families. Our acquisition is different. It is a plain brown work dress from about 1895, and it was worn by a servant in a large house.

Why would a museum want such an ordinary dress? The answer is its survival. Rich people's clothes were often kept in boxes for generations, so many of them have survived. A servant's dress, on the other hand, was worn every day until it fell apart, and then it was cut up and used to clean floors. The survival of a dress like this one is extremely rare. In fact, the absence of ordinary clothes is one of the biggest problems in museums like ours. Because of this absence, visitors can easily believe that everyone in the past dressed like a princess.

The dress is a survivor in another way, too. In 1921, a fire caused the destruction of most of the house where it was kept. Nobody was hurt, but the destruction was almost complete. Only one room on the ground floor remained, and in that room was a box with the dress inside. It is a true survivor: if you come very close, you can still notice a slight smell of smoke.

According to the auction house, the dress belonged to a young servant named Mary Collins. I must call her its alleged owner, since we have no photograph of her wearing it. However, the alleged owner left us something almost as good: a letter to her sister. In one passage of the letter, she writes about "my new brown dress, which the cook says makes me look very serious." When I read that passage for the first time, I had to sit down. It was as if a stranger had spoken to me across 130 years.

The dress will be on display from November. Next to it, we will show the letter, open at that passage, so that visitors can read Mary's words for themselves. The dress reminds us that history is made not only by kings and queens, but also by the people who washed their floors.

Questions:
What is the museum affiliated with?
It is affiliated with the state university.
Where did the museum buy the dress?
It bought the dress at an auction in Boston.
Why is the survival of a servant's dress so rare?
It is rare because servants wore their dresses every day until they fell apart.
How did the dress survive the destruction of the house?
It was in a box in the only room that remained after the fire.
Why does the writer call Mary Collins the alleged owner?
Because there is no photograph of Mary wearing the dress.
What does Mary write in one passage of her letter?
She writes that the cook says her new brown dress makes her look very serious.

lessons.title: What Is Your Shirt Made Of?
lessons.summary: A short informative text about where the materials of our clothes come from.
lessons.text:
Look at the label inside your shirt. There is a good chance that it says "100% cotton." Cotton is the most common natural material in our clothes.

Cotton grows on a plant. When the plant is ready, it opens and shows a soft white ball that looks a little like a cloud. The plant needs a lot of sun and water, and farmers must fight the weeds that grow between the rows. A field full of weeds can lose half of its cotton.

Wool comes from sheep, both from the females and from the males, which are called rams. A ram usually has thicker wool than a female, so farmers like to keep a few strong rams. Once a year, the sheep and the rams have their wool cut, which does not hurt them at all.

Cotton and wool are biological materials, which means that they come from living things. Biological materials have one great advantage: when they are thrown away, they slowly return to the earth. Many modern clothes, on the other hand, are made from plastic, which can stay in the ground for hundreds of years.

For most of history, people colored their clothes with vegetable dyes made from roots, leaves, flowers and even the skins of onions. Vegetable colors are softer than modern ones. To fix the color, a small dose of salt is added to the water. Too small a dose, and the color washes out; too large a dose, and the material can be damaged.

If you hold a shirt up to the light, you can also see its density, that is, how close together the threads are. Material with a high density is stronger and lasts longer, while material with a low density is lighter and cooler. Density also explains why some shirts become smaller in the drum of the washing machine: when a loose material gets hot in the drum, its threads move closer together.

Some scientists are even studying spiders. The thread that a spider uses for its web is light and, for its weight, stronger than steel. Nobody can keep spiders the way we keep sheep, but perhaps one day we will wear shirts inspired by them.

Clothing has always been a part of commerce. For centuries, ships carried cotton and wool across the oceans, and whole cities grew rich from this commerce. Today, the cotton for a single shirt may be grown in one country, colored in another and made into a shirt in a third. The label in your shirt tells only a small part of a very long story.

Questions:
Why must farmers fight the weeds in cotton fields?
Because a field full of weeds can lose half of its cotton.
What is the advantage of biological materials?
When they are thrown away, they slowly return to the earth.
What did people use to make vegetable dyes?
They used roots, leaves, flowers and the skins of onions.
Why must the dose of salt be right?
If the dose is too small, the color washes out, and if it is too large, the material can be damaged.
Why can a shirt become smaller in the drum of a washing machine?
Because when a loose material gets hot, its threads move closer together.

lessons.title: Costumes for an Epic
lessons.summary: A drama teacher, her students and their parents make costumes for a school play written in verse.
lessons.text:
Every spring, the oldest students at Lincoln Middle School put on a play. This year, the drama teacher, Mrs. Hill, chose something unusual: an epic poem called The Rider of the Stars. It was written by a local poet, Agnes Moore, who had worked for 30 years in publishing before she began to write her own books. A small publishing company in our city printed the poem two years ago, and the poet herself gave permission for the play.

The epic tells the story of a young rider, a girl on a white horse, who travels across the galaxy to bring back the sun, which has gone out. It is written entirely in verse, so the students had to learn their lines in verse, too. At first they complained. "Nobody talks in verse," said one boy. After a few weeks, however, the rhythm of the verse helped them remember their lines, and some students even began to speak in verse in the halls, just for fun.

The biggest challenge was the costumes. An epic needs a lot of costumes: kings, queens, stars, clouds and, of course, the rider herself. The school had very little money, so Mrs. Hill asked parents for old clothes and spare material. Every Wednesday after school, a group of students and parents met in the art room to work.

The rider's costume was simple: white pants, a long white coat and a cape the color of gold. The galaxy costumes were more difficult. Ten students played the galaxy itself, moving slowly around the rider while she rode through space. For their costumes, a group of mothers dyed old sheets a deep, dark blue. Then the students added thousands of tiny silver stars. When the lights went down, the ten students looked like a real galaxy turning in the night.

Because the school had no stage large enough, the play took place in the town's small sports arena. The arena usually hosted basketball games, so the students covered the floor with black material. On the night of the show, nearly 600 people came, and the arena was full.

The poet sat in the first row. When the rider finally brought the sun back, a bright yellow light filled the arena, and the audience stood up and cheered for several minutes. Afterward, Agnes Moore went to the art room to thank the students. She held up one of the galaxy costumes and looked at the little silver stars. "When I wrote this poem," she said, "I imagined it exactly like this. I just never imagined it in a basketball arena."

Questions:
Who wrote The Rider of the Stars?
It was written by a local poet, Agnes Moore.
What did Agnes Moore do before she began to write her own books?
She worked for 30 years in publishing.
What is the epic about?
It is about a young rider who travels across the galaxy to bring back the sun.
How did the verse help the students?
The rhythm of the verse helped them remember their lines.
How were the galaxy costumes made?
Mothers dyed old sheets dark blue, and the students added tiny silver stars.
Where did the play take place?
It took place in the town's small sports arena.

lessons.title: Packing for a Cruise
lessons.summary: A fashion columnist helps her mother, a retired nurse, choose clothes for her first cruise.
lessons.text:
Packing for a Cruise
By Nora Evans

Dear reader, this week's column is a little personal. My mother, Grace, worked as a nurse at a children's clinic for 35 years. She was the kind of nurse who remembered every child's name and every child's favorite color. When she retired last year, the whole clinic came to her party, and a little boy gave her a drawing of herself with wings.

Since then, my mother has lived carefully on her pension. For a whole year, she saved a small part of her pension every month, and in May she is going on her very first cruise. The ship will sail along the coast for ten days, and she is as excited as a child.

Last week she called me with a question. "You write about clothes for a living," she said. "So tell me: what does a person wear on a cruise?" I suspect that more than one reader has the same question, so here is my advice.

First, think in layers. On a cruise, the weather can change several times a day. The deck can be hot in the middle of the day and cold in the evening. A light cotton shirt, a warm sweater and a thin jacket that stops the wind will cover almost every situation.

Second, bring comfortable shoes. Walking on a moving ship tires the legs more than you would expect. My mother spent decades on her feet at the clinic, so she does not tire easily, but even she agreed that her new shoes should be soft and flat.

Third, pack one special outfit. Most cruises have at least one formal dinner, and it is fun to dress up. A simple dark dress or a good suit is enough. There is no need to buy anything expensive.

Finally, leave some space in your bag, in case you want to bring home a gift or two.

When I asked my followers online for their advice, I received more than 300 answers in a single day. One follower recommended a hat that ties under the chin, "unless you want to watch it fly into the ocean." Another follower, a woman who has been on 14 cruises, wrote that the most important thing to pack is curiosity. I think she is right.

My mother has now packed her bag three times, just to be sure. I will tell you, dear reader, how her cruise goes when she returns.

Questions:
Where did Grace work for 35 years?
She worked as a nurse at a children's clinic.
How did Grace pay for her cruise?
She saved a small part of her pension every month for a whole year.
Why does Nora recommend thinking in layers?
Because the weather on a cruise can change several times a day.
Why are comfortable shoes important on a cruise?
Because walking on a moving ship tires the legs more than you would expect.
What did one follower recommend?
She recommended a hat that ties under the chin.
What did the woman who had been on 14 cruises say?
She said that the most important thing to pack is curiosity.
